parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Smoke particles are suspended in still air. Brownian motion of the smoke particles is seen through a microscope.

Describe:
parts.text: what is seen through the microscope
hints: Hint 1: Picture looking down the microscope in a dark room - you cannot see air molecules, but you can see tiny bright spots where light scatters off the much larger smoke particles, and the air itself is still.
parts.proper_answer: Bright specks of light seen moving haphazardly in random zig-zag motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What you actually see**
Think of shining a torch on dust. You do not see the air, you see bright points where light reflects off the smoke particles against a dark background. Each speck is one smoke particle.

Step 2: **How they move**
Even though the air is still with no wind or current, those specks never sit still. They jitter about in a random, haphazard zig-zag path, constantly changing speed and direction. That random jitter is Brownian motion.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: how Brownian motion provides evidence for the nature of the movement of gas molecules.

markscheme_points.text: or random motion of the (gas) molecules causes the (haphazard) motion of the smoke particles or causes the smoke particles to change direction

hints: Hint 1: Remember the huge size difference - smoke particles are visible and heavy, air molecules are invisible, tiny and very fast. What must be hitting the smoke to make it jitter if the air as a whole is still?

Hint 2: Link the visible haphazard motion to the invisible motion - if the kicks from different sides are uneven and constantly changing, what does that tell you about how the air molecules themselves are moving?
parts.proper_answer: Invisible air molecules collide with the visible smoke particles. The random motion of the air molecules causes unbalanced bombardment, making the smoke particles move haphazardly.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Invisible kicks**
Air is made of molecules moving at hundreds of metres per second. You cannot see them, but they are constantly bombarding the much larger smoke particles from all sides.

Step 2: **Why the motion is random**
At any instant more molecules may hit from one side than another, giving a net kick in that direction. A moment later the imbalance is in a different direction. So the smoke particle is knocked into a zig-zag path.

Step 3: **The evidence**
Since the smoke moves randomly and continuously, the air molecules hitting it must also be moving randomly and continuously. This is direct visual evidence for the kinetic idea that gas molecules are in constant random motion.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A fixed mass of an ideal gas has volume $2.40 \times 10^3 \text{cm}^3$ at pressure $3.51 \times 10^5 \text{Pa}$ and temperature $290\text{K}$. The gas is heated at constant volume until the temperature is $310\text{K}$ at pressure $3.75 \times 10^5 \text{Pa}$, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1

The quantity of thermal energy required to raise the temperature of $1.00\text{mol}$ of the gas by $1.00\text{K}$ at constant volume is $12.5\text{J}$.

Calculate, to three significant figures:
parts.text: the amount, in mol, of the gas
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the link between the measurable state of a fixed mass of gas - its pressure, volume and absolute temperature - and the number of moles present.

Hint 2: Check your units before substituting - volume must be in $\text{m}^3$ so convert $2.40 \times 10^3 \text{ cm}^3$, and use $R = 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}$ with $p$ in $\text{Pa}$ and $T$ in $\text{K}$.
Hint 3: Rearrange to make amount the subject and use either the initial state $3.51 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$, $290 \text{ K}$ or the final state, both give the same $n$ to three significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Governing law**
For a fixed mass of ideal gas the state is described by: $$pV = nRT$$ where $p$ is pressure, $V$ is volume, $n$ is amount in mol, $R = 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}$ and $T$ is absolute temperature.

Step 2: **Prepare SI units**
$$V = 2.40 \times 10^3 \text{ cm}^3 = 2.40 \times 10^3 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3 = 2.40 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$$ Pressure and temperature are already in $\text{Pa}$ and $\text{K}$.

Step 3: **Substitute and calculate**
Rearrange for $n$: $$n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$ Using the initial state: $$n = \frac{(3.51 \times 10^5) \times (2.40 \times 10^{-3})}{8.31 \times 290} = \frac{842.4}{2409.9} \approx 0.350 \text{ mol}$$ Using the final state gives $0.349 \text{ mol}$, same to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the thermal energy transfer during the change.
hints: Hint 1: Think how the given figure of $12.5 \text{ J}$ per mole per kelvin scales up - it depends on how many moles you have from the last part and how many kelvin the temperature rises.
Hint 2: Find the temperature rise from $290 \text{ K}$ to $310 \text{ K}$ and multiply amount $\times$ energy per mole per kelvin $\times$ temperature rise.
parts.proper_answer: Thermal energy transfer $= 87.5 \text{ J}$ (accept $87.3 \text{ J}$ using $0.349 \text{ mol}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Scaling the molar energy**
Heating at constant volume means all heat goes to internal kinetic energy. For $n$ moles and rise $\Delta T$: $$\Delta Q = n \times 12.5 \times \Delta T$$

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$\Delta T = 310 - 290 = 20.0 \text{ K}$$ $$\Delta Q = 0.350 \times 12.5 \times 20.0 = 0.350 \times 250 = 87.5 \text{ J}$$ This is the thermal energy supplied during the change.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: For the change in the gas in (b), state:
parts.text: the quantity of external work done on the gas
hints: Hint 1: Recall that external work needs a volume change to push against external pressure - look at Fig. 2.1 and see what happens to volume between start and finish.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why no work**
Mechanical work by or on a gas is $W = p\Delta V$. Here the gas is heated at constant volume, so: $$\Delta V = 0$$ There is no expansion or compression, no distance moved against pressure, so external work done is zero.

hints: Hint 1: Recall that external work needs a volume change to push against external pressure - look at Fig. 2.1 and see what happens to volume between start and finish.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the change in internal energy, with the direction of this change.
hints: Hint 1: Use the first law $\Delta U = q + w$ - you already know the heat supplied in (b)(ii) and the work from (c)(i).
Hint 2: Decide the sign from temperature - if temperature rises from $290 \text{ K}$ to $310 \text{ K}$, average molecular kinetic energy and hence internal energy must go up or down?
parts.proper_answer: Change $= 87.5 \text{ J}$ (accept $87.3 \text{ J}$), direction is increase.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply the first law**
$$\Delta U = q + w$$ where $q$ is thermal energy supplied to the gas and $w$ is work done on the gas. Here $w = 0$ and $q = +87.5 \text{ J}$, so: $$\Delta U = +87.5 \text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Direction**
Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. Temperature has risen, molecules move faster on average, so internal energy increases by the full amount of heat supplied.
